references.title: Competitive Advantage: Creating and Sustaining Superior Performance
references.summary: The value chain: primary activities (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service) and support activities (firm infrastructure, human resource management, technology development, procurement).

stance.why: Each department is tagged primary or support by Porter's activities, and the optional grouping folders take those names; product development is filed as primary for a venture whose product is its work.

references.title: APQC Process Classification Framework (PCF), cross-industry and industry-specific versions
references.summary: A hierarchical taxonomy of business processes with 13 top-level categories (from Develop Vision and Strategy to Develop and Manage Business Capabilities), published cross-industry and in industry-specific versions. Each element has a hierarchy id, which can change between versions, and a five-digit element id, which does not. Version 8.0 (March 2026), cross-industry, has 13 categories, 74 process groups, 363 processes, 1,352 activities and 215 tasks; Naive carries its levels 1 to 5 in packages/naive/src/functions/pcf.json. Its licence, printed in each of APQC's 13 Definitions and Key Measures articles for version 8.0: "The Process Classification Framework is the copyrighted intellectual property of APQC. APQC encourages the wide distribution, discussion, and use of the PCF for classifying and defining organizational processes. Accordingly, APQC hereby grants you a perpetual, worldwide, royalty-free license to use, copy, publish, modify, and create derivative works of the PCF, provided that all copies of the PCF and any derivative works contain the following attribution: APQC’s Process Classification Framework® (PCF) is an open standard developed by APQC, a nonprofit that promotes benchmarking and best practices worldwide. The PCF is intended to facilitate organizational improvement through process management and benchmarking, regardless of industry, size, or geography. To download the full PCF or industry-specific versions of the PCF, as well as associated measures and benchmarking, please visit www.apqc.org/pcf."

stance.why: A venture's departments are the PCF's top-level categories under short ids, and the tool and activity catalogs file their entries under its process groups and processes. Naive ships the cross-industry element names of version 8.0 as data under APQC's licence, with the attribution it requires, and none of APQC's definitions or measures.

references.title: SciNet: The Anatomy of Science
references.summary: A database of the tasks researchers perform across all scientific disciplines, modeled on O*NET: 7,262 task statements in 10 categories, grouped into 140 work activities and broken into 90,583 steps, each placed in a context (all research, or one of 6 domains, 34 fields and 318 subfields) and scored on importance, share of researchers, frequency and descriptive dimensions. Release v1.10.0, repository https://github.com/lukasalthoff/scinet, licensed CC BY 4.0.

stance.why: Naive takes SciNet's method and choice of scales, not its research tasks: an activity is a task statement in O*NET form, the catalog grows by adding a statement and checking it, work is placed on one axis and context on another, and activities are scored on the CDR, RL feasibility and O*NET scales SciNet uses. Any statement taken from SciNet cites it with source.ref, as CC BY 4.0 requires.

references.title: O*NET OnLine
authors: US Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration
references.summary: The US occupational database: each occupation's tasks as task statements (a verb, its object and, where useful, how or why), rated for importance (1 to 5), relevance (the percent of incumbents who report the task) and frequency (seven categories from yearly or less to hourly or more).

stance.why: An activity's statement follows the O*NET task statement structure, and the importance, share and frequency scales are O*NET's importance, relevance and frequency scales.

references.title: O*NET Database, text release
authors: US Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration
references.summary: The O*NET database as tab-delimited files, one release at a time: release 31.0 (August 2026) has 1,016 occupations by O*NET-SOC code and title in Occupation Data.txt, 2,087 detailed work activities (DWAs) under 332 intermediate and 41 generalized work activities in GWAs to IWAs to DWAs.txt, and the links from each occupation's task statements to DWAs in Tasks to DWAs.txt. Licensed under CC BY 4.0 (https://www.onetcenter.org/license_db.html), which asks a copy to say it includes information from the O*NET database by USDOL/ETA, used under CC BY 4.0, and, when modified, that USDOL/ETA has not approved, endorsed, or tested the modifications.

stance.why: O*NET is the reference for which roles are missing (EE-232): Naive carries each occupation's code and title and its work activity links, with O*NET's attribution, and suggests occupations for a PCF element no role answers for. A role's onet field names an occupation from it with who matched it and on what basis.

references.title: Measuring AI's Economic Reach: A Multi-Dimensional Task Taxonomy
references.summary: The CDR taxonomy (GWU Center for Economic Research working paper 2026-005): three ordinal axes for a task, Cognitive complexity (C0 to C4), Deployment difficulty (D0 to D4) and Regulatory restrictions (R0 to R4), applied to the O*NET task universe.

stance.why: The cognitive-complexity, physical-deployment and regulatory-restriction scales are the CDR axes with their 0 to 4 levels, because they separate whether a task can be done from whether it can be deployed and whether institutions permit it.

references.title: What Jobs Can AI Learn? Measuring Exposure by Reinforcement Learning
references.summary: The RL Feasibility Index (arXiv 2605.02598): every O*NET task scored on eight dimensions of reinforcement learning training feasibility, each from 1 to 10; dimension D1, verification method, runs from contested expert judgment with no inspectable artifact (1) to a fully deterministic programmatic check (10).

stance.why: The verification scale is the index's verification method dimension, on its 1 to 10 range: how an activity's result can be checked bears on what evidence a handoff can ask for.

references.title: ISO/IEC 25010:2023 Systems and software engineering, Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE), Product quality model
references.summary: The product quality model: nine characteristics a system's quality is judged by (functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, interaction capability, reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility and safety), each with subcharacteristics.

stance.why: Each language rubric criterion names the quality characteristics it serves, so the rubric judges a language by what it does to the system's quality. The licence criterion names none, because the standard does not cover licences.

references.title: TypeScript Design Goals
references.summary: The TypeScript project's goals and non-goals. Non-goal 3: "Apply a sound or 'provably correct' type system. Instead, strike a balance between correctness and productivity."

stance.why: The correctness criterion scores TypeScript's types as static but unsound by design, from the project's own non-goal.

references.title: Theorem Proving in Lean 4
references.summary: The introduction to Lean 4 as a theorem prover and a programming language, based on a version of dependent type theory powerful enough to prove almost any conventional mathematical theorem.

stance.why: The correctness criterion's top level is a machine-checked proof, which is what Lean gives and where Naive proves its definitions (EE-095).

references.title: Effect documentation
references.summary: Effect, a TypeScript library for building production-grade software: failures are typed values in the signature, services are wired through the type system and swapped in tests, and effects run with bounded, structured concurrency. Naive pins it exactly (EE-125).

stance.why: The effects and concurrency criterion's top level describes what Effect gives Naive: failures, dependencies and concurrency in the types, and a service a test replaces.

references.title: Node.js documentation: Modules: TypeScript
references.summary: Node.js runs TypeScript files that contain only erasable syntax by replacing the types with whitespace, with no type checking; enums, namespaces with runtime code, parameter properties and import aliases are not supported. To discourage publishing packages written in TypeScript, Node.js refuses to handle TypeScript files under a node_modules path.

stance.why: The runtime fit and operability criteria use it to show one language can fit a target in one place and not another, which is why Naive compiles on publish (EE-159).

references.title: WebAssembly
references.summary: WebAssembly (Wasm) is a binary instruction format for a stack-based virtual machine, designed as a portable compilation target for programming languages. Embedded in the web it keeps the browser's same-origin and permissions policies, and it also supports non-web embeddings.

stance.why: The runtime fit criterion counts a language that reaches a browser or another host only by compiling to WebAssembly as fitting through a compile step, not as written.

references.title: JSON Schema specification, draft 2020-12
references.summary: The JSON Schema core and validation vocabularies, current version 2020-12. Every Naive record type has a schema in this draft.

stance.why: The interop criterion asks whether a language can validate Naive's records against these schemas, since every record is JSON checked by one.

references.title: Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems
references.summary: How Google builds, releases, monitors and runs production systems, including release engineering and the cost of toil.

stance.why: The operability criterion counts build, release and debugging work on every release as a cost of the language, as the book counts release engineering and toil.

references.title: SPDX License List
references.summary: Commonly used open source licences and exceptions, each with a standard identifier, full name and FSF and OSI status. MIT and Apache-2.0 are listed as OSI approved.

stance.why: The licence criterion names licences by SPDX identifier, and its top level is a permissive OSI-approved licence.

references.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data (General Data Protection Regulation)
authors: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
references.summary: Article 5 holds personal data to purpose limitation, data minimisation and storage limitation; article 6 requires a lawful basis for processing; article 7 sets the conditions for consent and the right to withdraw it; article 13 requires that the person be told, including how long the data is kept; article 17 gives the right to erasure.

stance.why: The visibility rubric's consent-and-retention criterion is a gate because recording a person needs a lawful basis they were told about, a retention period and a way to erase. No URL is recorded here because none was checked in this change.
